body.text: In short:
Mr Xi said there had been a "full turnaround" in relations between Australia and China since Anthony Albanese became prime minister.
What's next?
Mr Albanese will travel to Beijing for further meetings with senior officials.
Chinese President Xi Jinping has declared Australia and China have had a "full turnaround" in relations "despite differences" in the past four years under the Albanese government.
Mr Xi made the remarks at the opening of a meeting with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen today.
"We have jointly promoted the full turnaround of China-Australia relations, and exchanges and cooperation in various fields between our two countries have continued to deepen," Mr Xi said.

"I will work with you in the spirit of equality, seeking common ground despite differences, and mutually beneficial cooperation to take forward the China-Australia Comprehensive Strategic Partnership."
Mr Albanese said the Australia-China relationship "delivers prosperity for both of our countries" but promised "frank" conversations.
"And the relationship that we are building is positive, is calm, is not defined by our differences, but one where we can have clear and frank exchanges for our mutual interest," he said.
It's the fifth meeting between the pair since Mr Albanese came to office in 2022.
At that time relations had plunged to their lowest point in decades, with Beijing imposing trade restrictions on Australian exports and high-level talks between the two countries effectively frozen.

Mr Albanese is due to travel to Beijing tonight for formal talks with Chinese Premier Li Qiang and the Australia-China CEO roundtable where businesses are expected to push for greater trade certainty.
Albanese says government 'worked hard' to stabilise relationship

Speaking after his meeting with Mr Xi, Mr Albanese said his government had "worked hard to stabilise the relationship" with China "for the interests of our relationship with our major trading partner".
Mr Albanese said he discussed a full range of issues with Mr Xi.
"It is important that Australia continue to engage in a constructive way with China, manage our differences, but not be defined by them," he said.

Asked whether China's longer term ambitions meant differences between the countries would endure, Mr Albanese said the two countries were able to discuss those issues "constructively and very directly".
"That's something that we do in meetings," he said.
"We have different political systems, different histories, but that doesn't mean that you can't have constructive dialogue, and that's what Australia seeks."
"It is always better to have dialogue than to have conflict," he said.
On confronting Mr Putin over Ukraine during his APEC speech, Mr Albanese said he had made it "very clear" Russia needed to stop the war.
"Well, he certainly heard it, as did others in the room," Mr Albanese said.
"I have a responsibility to put Australia's position clearly and directly, and that is what I did."
China talks follow Australia's deals on defence, AI
The high-level talks come after Australia signed a series of agreements that Beijing is unlikely to welcome.

Just days before arriving in China, Mr Albanese oversaw the signing of a new defence cooperation agreement with the Philippines aimed at strengthening military ties, maritime surveillance and information sharing.
He reiterated Australia's support for Manila, which has repeatedly clashed with Beijing over disputed territorial claims in the South China Sea.

Mr Albanese also joined Mr Trump, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi for a Quad summit in the Philippines, where the four leaders announced plans for a new joint exercise in the region next year.

This same week, Australia signed a US-led agreement aimed at protecting the technology and supply chains needed to develop advanced AI, as Washington seeks to reduce its reliance on China for critical minerals and strengthen its position in the global technology race.
The moves highlight the balancing act facing Mr Albanese ahead of his meetings with the highest levels of Chinese leadership where he will seek to expand economic cooperation.
Australian businesses call for 'certainty' in trade with China
Meanwhile, Australia's biggest businesses are pushing for more certainty in their dealings with China as global tensions threaten to disrupt trade and investment.
Executives from BHP, Rio Tinto, ANZ and other major companies will meet their Chinese counterparts in Beijing on Friday seeking better access to local markets and assurances of fair competition.
The Business Council of Australia (BCA) has confirmed it will push for greater access to China's agricultural markets, including for beef and rice exports.

In addition to agricultural market access, the Australian business delegation in Beijing will also use the talks to seek the removal of trade barriers facing Australian medical technology companies, including hearing implant manufacturer Cochlear, and improve recognition of Australian professional qualifications.
Artificial intelligence is on the agenda, with Australian and Chinese business leaders looking to deepen cooperation on the technology despite global competition over its development.
The BCA wants companies to explore how AI could improve agricultural productivity, including using farm-level and supply chain data.
Resources will also be a focus, with mining giants BPH and Rio Tinto joining discussions on how Australia and China can work together to cut emissions from steel production.

In a speech at the CEO roundtable in Beijing, BCA president Geoff Culbert will warn geopolitical shifts and changing trade patterns are creating new challenges for companies trying to make long-term investment decisions.
"Companies make decisions today that will shape their businesses for years and decades to come," he will say.
"Those decisions depend on having confidence in the markets where we operate, the partners we work with and the rules that govern our investments."
Mr Culbert will say business confidence relies on "trust and predictability".
"Australia strongly supports an open trading system and effective international rules, I which openness goes hand in hand with fair competition and a level playing field," he will say.
